surveyDefinition.title: Skin Care Products — consumer survey (China)
surveyDefinition.studyPurpose: Identify which of 4 behavioural segments each respondent belongs to, based on skin care routine complexity, product format usage, purchase drivers, and openness to clinical-grade at-home solutions.

segments.name: High-Commitment Routine Users
segments.description: Use 5+ steps daily, invest significant time and money, follow multi-step regimens, often K-beauty inspired, driven by visible results and sensory experience.

segments.name: Targeted Treatment Buyers
segments.description: Use fewer steps but highly purposeful, focused on specific concerns (aging, hyperpigmentation, hormonal changes), willing to pay for clinical efficacy and dermatologist-recommended products.

segments.name: Value-Driven Basic Users
segments.description: Use minimal routine (cleanser, moisturizer, sunscreen), price-sensitive, buy on promotion, switch frequently for better price, less engaged with claims.

segments.name: Preventive Maintenance Users
segments.description: Use a moderate routine (3-4 steps) focused on maintaining healthy skin, not treating specific problems, brand-loyal, value convenience and trusted brands.

surveyDefinition.whatThisSurveyIs: A segmentation study of Skin Care Products buyers in China. It asks how people use Skin Care Products, how they choose it, and what would make them switch — then sorts respondents into the behavioural groups defined below. Questions stay at category level: no named brands, and nothing about adjacent categories.
surveyDefinition.whoseContextThisIs: Adults in China who buy or use Skin Care Products for personal or household use. Respondents qualify if they: Individuals who have purchased at least one skin care product for personal use in the past 12 months; Primary decision-maker for their own skin care purchases; Ages 18 and older. Excluded: Professional buyers (e.g., dermatology clinics, spas, salons) purchasing for resale or professional use; Individuals purchasing solely as gifts for others; Children under 18.
surveyDefinition.whyTheseRespondents: Everyday consumers buy skin care products for personal use, pay for them out of pocket at retail or online, and make the purchase decision themselves. While some professional products are sold to salons, the dominant consumer market is direct-to-consumer, so this is a pure B2C segment.
respondentBehaviours: Regularly purchases skin care products (e.g., cleansers, moisturizers, serums, sunscreens)
Researches products online, reads reviews, follows influencers or dermatologist recommendations
May have specific skin concerns (acne, aging, sensitivity, hyperpigmentation)
Brand loyal but open to switching for better efficacy or price
Purchases through multiple channels: drugstores, department stores, specialty beauty retailers, e-commerce, subscription boxes
whatIsDeliberatelyNotAsked: Age or household income as behavioural questions — no finding in this survey is driven by them. They are asked once, at the end, in Profiling, and used only to cross-tabulate the behavioural results.
Brand, company or manufacturer names — the survey stays at category level so findings are not tied to one competitor set.
Where the respondent lives — region is chosen when viewing the results, so asking it again would waste a question.
surveyDefinition.howToReadTheNumbers: Percentages are modelled estimates built from published market evidence — they are not measurements from fielded interviews, and should be read as an expected shape of response rather than a result. Single-choice, ranking and rating-scale questions sum to 100%. Multi-select questions do not — each option is an independent share of respondents choosing it. The N shown on each question is the display base for that item.

structure.storyline: Questions run in a planned narrative order: broad and easy first, specific and sensitive last.
structure.storylineSummary: The survey opens by mapping the respondent's current skin care routine — how many steps, which formats, how often — and the skin concerns that drive it. It then follows the purchase journey: what triggers a buy, where they research and shop, how much they spend, and which factors (efficacy, price, brand, dermatologist advice) actually decide the choice. Next it probes what they demand from a product — must-have attributes, quality cues, packaging preferences, and the trade-offs they will accept — before closing on satisfaction, unmet needs, switching triggers, and openness to future…

metadata.studyPurpose: Identify which of 4 behavioural segments each respondent belongs to, based on skin care routine complexity, product format usage, purchase drivers, and openness to clinical-grade at-home solutions.
metadata.segmentation_lens: Usage/Behavioural combined with Jobs-to-be-Done: the axis that separates buyers is the complexity of their routine and the primary job their skin care is hired to do (preventive maintenance vs. targeted treatment vs. cost-managed basics vs. clinical-grade results). segmentModel.tie_break: Question cp4 (main reason for using skincare) is the most direct behavioural self-report: choosing 'To treat a current skin concern' clearly separates targeted treatment seekers from preventive maintainers who choose 'To prevent future skin problems' or 'To maintain healthy-looking skin', and from routine enthusiasts who choose 'To relax and enjoy the experience'.
notes: Routine enthusiasts are identified by high step/product counts, both AM/PM application, sensory enjoyment, and interest in devices/peels.
Targeted treatment seekers are identified by concern-driven behaviour, clinical efficacy focus, dermatologist influence, and willingness to pay for results.
Value-driven basic users are identified by minimal routine, price sensitivity, promotion-driven purchases, and willingness to switch for affordability.

Preventive maintainers are identified by moderate routine, prevention/maintenance motivation, convenience, and brand loyalty (though brand loyalty not directly asked, restock behaviour and satisfaction with convenience serve as proxies).
8 scoring weight(s) removed: they scored questions that were dropped as duplicates before publication.
segmentModel.excluded: Screening and Profiling questions are excluded from scoring: screeners carry no signal (everyone passed) and demographics are for cross-tabs, not segmentation.

fieldingNotes.recommendedSample: n=800-1,200 for stable segment-level sub-groups (roughly n>=312 per segment after weighting). At n=1,000 the margin of error on a whole-sample percentage is about ±3.1pp at 95% confidence; on a segment of n=200 it widens to about ±6.9pp, so segment-level differences under ~10pp should not be reported as real.
fieldingNotes.quotaControls: Apply quotas on the category-usage and frequency screeners so heavy users — who are more willing survey-takers — are not over-sampled.
scriptingNotes: Rotate the order of answer options on every non-ordinal question to remove primacy bias. Do NOT rotate ordinal scales (frequency bands, price bands, satisfaction) — their order carries meaning.
Anchor 'Other', 'None of these' and 'Prefer not to say' to the bottom of the list, exempt from rotation.
Every 'Other' option takes an open-text capture, coded back into the frame at analysis if any single verbatim exceeds 3%.
No routing or skip logic: every respondent sees every question, so the base is constant across the instrument.
Include one attention check in the middle third — a standard instructed-response item. Terminate on failure and replace.
Randomise the order of the two ranking/trade-off items between respondents so neither is systematically answered while fresher.
caveats: Percentages in this document are modelled from published market evidence, not measured from fielded interviews. Replace them with primary data once the study is run.
Ranking items are shown as a lighter-weight ranking exercise; run them as MaxDiff if you need more precision on driver importance.
Profiling questions are for cross-tabs only and are excluded from the segmentation scoring model.

metadata.storyline_summary: The survey opens by mapping the respondent's current skin care routine — how many steps, which formats, how often — and the skin concerns that drive it. It then follows the purchase journey: what triggers a buy, where they research and shop, how much they spend, and which factors (efficacy, price, brand, dermatologist advice) actually decide the choice. Next it probes what they demand from a product — must-have attributes, quality cues, packaging preferences, and the trade-offs they will accept — before closing on satisfaction, unmet needs, switching triggers, and openness to future…
storyline_notes: Added a beat on 'routine steps' in consumer_profile to capture the complexity that distinguishes High-Commitment Routine Users from Value-Driven Basic Users.
Included 'at-home devices' as a must-cover topic and in future_use to address the growing demand for non-invasive, clinical-grade solutions in the region.
Emphasized 'dermatologist recommendation' as a decision driver and quality cue, reflecting the trust in clinical efficacy in the market.
In preferences_expectations, added a beat on 'willingness to pay for results' to separate Luxury Anti-Aging Enthusiasts from Budget-Conscious Students.
In satisfaction_future_intent, added 'interest in future innovations' to capture the growing interest in menopause-specific and device-based products, aligning with the market profile.
metadata.classification_reason: Everyday consumers buy skin care products for personal use, pay for them out of pocket at retail or online, and make the purchase decision themselves. While some professional products are sold to salons, the dominant consumer market is direct-to-consumer, so this is a pure B2C segment.
